state.misconception_label: Thinks you can find missing values in a given table by treating the row as linear and adding on the difference between the first two values given.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: The equation \( f=3 r^{2}+3 \) is used to find values in the table below. What is the value covered by the star? \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline\( r \) & \( 1 \) & \( 2 \) & \( 3 \) & \( 4 \) \\ \hline\( f \) & \( 6 \) & \( 15 \) & \( \color{gold}\bigstar \) & \\ \hline \end{tabular}. I got \( 24 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you explain why you chose to add on the difference between the first two values in the table to find the missing value? How does the equation \( f=3 r^{2}+3 \) relate to the pattern you see in the table?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, so I looked at the first two values and saw that 15 minus 6 is 9, so I thought the pattern just kept adding 9 each time, which gave me 24. But I'm not really sure how the equation f=3r²+3 is supposed to help me... does it mean I should be using the r values instead of just looking at the differences?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of a way to connect the equation f=3r²+3 with the values in the table to help you find the missing value? How might the relationship between r and f in the equation guide your approach to solving for the value covered by the star?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I think I see what you mean now - so I should plug in the r value into the equation instead of just looking at the differences? So like, when r is 3, I'd do f = 3 times 3 squared plus 3, which would be 3 times 9 plus 3... so that's 27 plus 3 which equals 30? Is that how you're supposed to use the equation to find the missing value?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher directly addresses the linear addition misconception by prompting the student to connect the equation to the table values, successfully guiding the student from incorrect pattern-spotting to correct substitution into the quadratic equation.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student toward understanding without ever directly providing the answer, helping the student discover that they should substitute r=3 into the equation rather than relying on pattern differences.
